explanation: The light-blue countries are the Global North (the IMF list of advanced economies), characterised by high per-capita income, strong economies and developed infrastructure [M4 s7].
The North/South split is socio-economic, not purely geographic (Australia is in the Global North), so it follows level of development rather than latitude or climate [M4 s6].
'The commons' are materials and/or resources that are used, owned and maintained together (water, air, forest, but also shared knowledge) [M4 s10, s11].

Subak is a man-made, culturally embedded commons: shared water managed through collective rules, rituals and Tri Hita Karana, i.e. a social-cultural (intellectual) institution rather than a marine or digital commons [M4 s12, s24].
note: The slides do not classify Subak into one of these four labels. They list the irrigation system among man-made commons (M4 s12) and traditional knowledge/culture as an intellectual commons (M4 s11); Subak is presented as a collective social-cultural institution (M4 s24). 'Intellectual' is the best fit by elimination, but 'biotic' (water, paddy) is arguable.

explanation: The MEA (2005) groups ecosystem services into provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural; 'industrial' is not a category [M4 s14].
Nutrient cycling underlies all other services and is a supporting service; the forest example on the slide lists 'support energy flow and chemical cycling' [M4 s16].
note: The Gersmehl diagram itself is not in the slides; nutrient cycling is the standard MEA example of a supporting service, and the forest slide lists 'support energy flow and chemical cycling' (M4 s16).

explanation: Climate regulation (rainfall, humidity, temperature stability) is a regulating service; the slide lists 'influence local and regional climate' and 'store atmospheric carbon' for forests [M4 s14, s16].
Spiritual and religious values attached to sacred places such as mountains are cultural services (non-material benefits) [M4 s14].
Material or energy products taken directly from nature (here coal as an energy source) are provisioning services [M4 s14].
On the Spoolman & Miller chart forests are the highest terrestrial value (US$15.6 trillion) and coastal marshes/mangroves the highest aquatic value (US$24.8 trillion) [M4 s17].
PES is the economic route in which beneficiaries of nature (e.g. downstream industry) pay those who preserve or enhance the service (e.g. upstream forest farmers), as in Cidanau [M4 s18].
Consumption of ozone-depleting substances (CFCs etc.) collapses after 1989, the result of the Montreal Protocol (1987) that banned them [M4 s21].
In Dieselgate VW used software that controlled emissions during testing, so on-road NOx emissions were about 20x higher; millions of vehicles were recalled [M4 s25].
The slide states that vehicle gas emissions in Indonesia refer to Permen LHK No. 8/2023 and PP No. 22/2021 [M4 s26].
The SDGs have 17 goals (2015–2030); the MDGs (2000–2015) had eight [M5 s3, s4].
17 goals and 169 targets; 231 indicators apply globally and Indonesia has 289 tailored to its development targets [M5 s8].
Access to 5G/digital connectivity is infrastructure and innovation, which is SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure); the slides link STI to SDG 9 and 17 [M5 s26].
note: 5G coverage (digital infrastructure and its uneven spread) is SDG 9 Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure; the slides do not discuss this map itself.

explanation: Harm to marine life and coral is SDG 14 Life Below Water (Goal 14 covers marine ecosystems) [M5 s18, s20].

SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) includes strengthening prevention and treatment of substance/narcotic drug abuse; the other options are targets of SDG 2, SDG 10/17 and SDG 8 (general knowledge, not on the slides) [M5 s6, s8].
note: Target 3.5 of the UN SDGs (substance and narcotic drug abuse) is general knowledge; the slides do not list SDG 3 targets.

explanation: SDG 16 is Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions [M7 s5].
SDG 11 is Sustainable Cities and Communities (SDG 4 is Quality Education, 13 Climate Action, 6 Clean Water and Sanitation) [M5 s6].
SDG 7 is Affordable and Clean Energy (SDG 12 Responsible Consumption and Production, 15 Life on Land, 17 Partnerships for the Goals) [M5 s8].
The IBSAP 2025–2045 vision is 'Living in harmony with nature for the sustainability of all life forms in Indonesia' [M5 s19].
Innovation is defined as a new way of producing, distributing or using goods and services based on new technology, new business models or new forms of economic/social organisation [M5 s23].
In the Addis Ababa Action Agenda, STI (including mutually agreed technology transfer) promotes sustainable development [M5 s24].
The slide pairs 'the challenges of each SDG require different STI' with knowledge management needs, and 'each country will generate and require different STI' with place-based priorities [M5 s27].

Of 140 targets evaluated 15% are on track, 48% are not, >30% stagnate or fall below 2015; more databases are compared and more agreed methods exist, so 'fewer agreed methods' is the false point [M5 s29].
The main components of the climate system (IPCC 2021) are atmosphere, biosphere, cryosphere and oceans; the anthroposphere is not one [M6 s3].
Methane (CH4) is the GHG typically associated with livestock (enteric fermentation) and rice farming; the cattle picture is the cue [M6 s4].
note: Livestock/agriculture as a methane source is general knowledge; the slides only list methane among the GHGs and do not tie it to livestock. N2O (fertiliser) is also agricultural, but the cattle picture points to CH4.

explanation: GWP measures the heat absorbed over a given period due to emission of a gas, with CO2 as the reference (GWP = 1) [M6 s6].
The Paris Agreement (adopted 2015, in force 2016) limits warming below 2°C while pursuing 1.5°C; the other options have impossible temperatures or dates [M6 s14, s19].
note: Entry into force in 2016 is general knowledge (the slides show the Paris Agreement as 2015–2030, adopted 2015); the goal text is 'well below 2°C, pursuing 1.5°C' (M6 s14 notes). Only option b is defensible.

explanation: Reviewing progress is the Global Stocktake, which belongs to the transparency principle, not to CBDR-RC (common, differentiated, respective capabilities) [M6 s16, s17].
The GST assesses collective progress and runs on a five-year cycle (first one concluded at COP28 in 2023) [M6 s12, s17].
note: The five-year GST cycle is Paris Agreement general knowledge; the slides describe the GST (first completed at COP28, 2023) but do not state the interval.

explanation: Sovereignty = bottom-up architecture: each country determines its own emission level and reports it as a Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) [M6 s18].

Indonesia's Enhanced NDC (2022) targets 31.89% unconditional and 43.2% with international support; the slides give 29%/41% for the original NDC and the same 31.89%/43.20% for the 2035 target of the 2nd NDC [M6 s19, s20].
note: Slide M6 s19 gives 29% / 41% for 2030 (the first NDC) and M6 s20 gives 31.89% / 43.20% for 2035 (second NDC). The 31.89% / 43.2% pair is the Enhanced NDC 2022 target for 2030, the only option matching the course's figures. No option shows 29/41, so c is the best answer, but the stem year and the slides' pairs do not align cleanly.

explanation: President Anote Tong's 'Migrate with Dignity' policy involved purchasing 6,000 acres in Fiji [M6 s23].
note: The stem says 2005; the slide dates Tong's statement to 2015. The paper's '6000 are' is a typo for 6,000 acres; the answer is unaffected.

explanation: Direct emissions are releases of high-GWP refrigerants (CFC, HCFC, HFC), e.g. leakage or poor handling during servicing; energy use is the indirect emission [M6 s28].
In 2019 energy produced 34% (20 GtCO2-eq), ahead of industry 24%, AFOLU 22% and transport 15% [M6 s32].
The slide's notes distinguish biological, geological and technological (e.g. direct air capture) sequestration; 'atmospherical' is not a type (the atmosphere is the source) [M6 s33].
CCUS works in sequence: capture the CO2, compress and transport it, then utilise or store it in geological formations, i.e. 3-2-1 [M6 s37].

Spillover effects occur when what one country consumes places stress (water, emissions, land conflict) on the producing country; high consumption with low production signals this cross-border transfer [M7 s4, s5].
SDGs are not achieved one by one; indivisibility means integrated within a common framework (alongside transformative and universality) [M7 s6].

Core (synergy) activities are education, public health, social/legal activities, renewable-energy transmission and distribution, and scientific research; cultural preservation through dance and painting is a peripheral activity [M7 s7, s10].
Single stream collects recyclables of mixed quality in one container; dual stream sorts by material quality to raise market value, so statements 1 and 4 are correct [M7 s11].
Indirect emissions embodied in energy, materials and trade are carried across borders as spillover effects, e.g. CO2 emissions and water stress in imports [M7 s4, s5].
note: Emission scopes 1-3 are not in the slides; the answer rests on the spillover concept (M7 s4-5), where emissions embodied in imports burden other countries. The stem also mislabels scope 1 as indirect.

explanation: Of the principles on the slide, indivisibility is 'integrated within a common framework', whereas universality is 'applicable in all countries' and transformative requires fundamental change [M7 s6].
note: Ambiguous stem: 'every country follows' hints at Universality (applicable in all countries) while 'integrated framework' matches Indivisibility (integrated within a common framework, M7 s6). The authors' key is Indivisibility.

explanation: Goals whose progress is often not reported are SDG 15, 14, 5 and 10; SDG 9, 11 and 12 are those that need attention instead [M7 s16].
The nexus approach deepens the integration between goals and targets across sectors, strengthening synergies and reducing trade-offs [M7 s21].
Boar et al. (2021): in the Global North synergies among SDGs include all three dimensions; in the Global South they cover only one dimension [M7 s17].
Responsible Innovation (Stilgoe et al.) rests on anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion and responsiveness; 'strategic' is not one of them [M7 s19].
